1:
The opening formula is read as deliberate. Delitzsch finds the didactic cast of the whole narrative already in its shape, since the chronicler drops the dated notice used in Kings for a loose connective, after these matters and this faithfulness, which Ellicott renders the same way. Gill and Clarke supply what it covers: the reformation settled, the throne secure, the Philistines beaten and the Assyrian yoke thrown off, Clarke adding that the pious king was left undisturbed until the work he had begun was finished. Wesley hears a warning rather than a reward: a man may be squarely in the way of duty and still meet trouble, which God permits to try his confidence.

Ellicott collects the forms of the invader's name in the Greek, Latin and Jewish sources, and sets against them the monumental Assyrian form, Sin-ahi-iriba, meaning that the moon-god has multiplied brothers. He also lets the man speak for himself, quoting the inscription: forty-six strong cities of Hezekiah of the country of the Jews, who had not submitted to the yoke, besides small towns without number, all taken.

That boast raises the question of what this account leaves out, and here the commentators divide. Clarke states the missing facts from Kings: in the fourteenth year the king of Judah first bought his enemy off with three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold, emptying his treasury and stripping the house of the Lord to do it. Ellicott agrees the tribute is absent and explains that by purpose: the chronicler means to relate a deliverance and omits whatever would weaken that impression. He reports Keil's further suggestion that the negotiations are left out as having no bearing on the issue of the war, and rejects the explanation of Thenius, that the writer shrank from recording a forced sacrilege, noting that Isaiah omits the episode too. Delitzsch insists the two accounts are not inconsistent.

On the waterworks Delitzsch observes that neither Kings nor Isaiah narrates them, though both confirm the fact elsewhere, and he presses the verb, which means not to block but to conceal, covering the springs and leading their water into underground channels. Wesley says the same in a clause: the water was drawn by secret pipes into the city. Both Delitzsch and Ellicott identify the stream so dried up as the Gihon, formed by the overflow of those springs; Ellicott places it in the valley of Hinnom, quotes a later encomium praising Hezekiah for bringing water into the city, and calls the plural kings of Assyria a rhetorical flourish. Clarke supplies the military sense, since a great army could not subsist in an arid country, and points to the crusaders of 1099 reduced to distress when the inhabitants stopped the wells against them.

The building notice contains a crux. Ellicott thinks a different division of the Hebrew letters gives raised towers upon it, and prefers that; Thenius keeps the received text and understands it as heightening the towers, arguing that the wall already had them; the Greek gives simply and towers, the Latin built towers above. Delitzsch merely records that the clause is obscure, since mounting the towers is meaningless and the causative leaves the sentence without an object. Ellicott takes the outer wall for the one enclosing the lower city and glosses Millo as the rampart. The address that follows is traced by Clarke and Ellicott alike to Elisha's words about the greater number on our side, Ellicott adding the borrowing from Jeremiah for the arm of flesh and cautioning that the chronicler gives the substance of the speech rather than its exact words. Gill reduces it to the contrast, weak mortal men on one side and the Lord on the other; Henry ends where Paul does, that if God is for us none can be against us, and that by his favour enemies are lost and friends gained.
9:
Gill and Clarke agree on what stands between the last paragraph and this: the tribute had been paid and the invader had withdrawn, and the embassy came afterwards, so the blasphemous message is a second and separate act. Ellicott suspects the ninth verse has lost a verb, since the clause about Lachish reads oddly without one, and thinks the word for army may have dropped from the phrase about his power, which means strictly his dominion. Against the silence of the great inscription on that siege he sets the relief in the British Museum, where the king sits enthroned while captives file out of a city gate, with the legend that Sennacherib, king of multitudes, king of Asshur, sat on a raised throne and caused the spoils of Lachish to pass before him.

Both close readers treat what follows as digest rather than transcript. Delitzsch says only the main ideas of the speech are reported, and Ellicott states plainly that these verses reproduce in brief the leading thoughts of the longer version in Kings. Both notice a softening: where the older account is coarse this one is not, Delitzsch remarking that the same thought is expressed far more grossly there. Ellicott renders the opening as a double question, on what are you trusting and why are you sitting in distress, and finds the idiom in Jeremiah.

Henry sorts the attack into two charges. Against the king it was an attempt to detach subjects from their allegiance by means unbecoming a crowned head, representing him as one who would deceive his people into ruin by famine and thirst, who had exposed them to divine displeasure by removing the high places and altars, and who held out against a force certain to destroy them. Ellicott supplies a contemporary parallel for the first of these from Esarhaddon, who boasts in the record of his Egyptian campaign that he built siege works and cut off food and water, the life of their souls. On that second point Ellicott makes a sharp observation about the chronicler's own hand: this account is even more emphatic than Kings that the one altar in the temple court is the only valid one, so the taunt lands on precisely the reform the writer most approves.

The second charge Henry calls impiety rather than malice. The blasphemer set the Maker of heaven and earth beside the dunghill gods of the nations, the work of men's hands, as though an infinite and eternal Spirit had no more wisdom or power than a stone or the stock of a tree; and having boasted that none of those gods protected their peoples, he argued not merely how shall your God deliver you but how much less, as if this one were feebler than all the rest. Delitzsch puts the logic in the same shape, that gods reckoned mightier had failed, so what could a lesser do. Ellicott explains why the reasoning seemed sound to those who used it: on the ancient view a strong nation had strong gods, and since Assyria had beaten nations stronger than Judah it supposed, in ignorance, that it had beaten stronger deities. He notes that some Hebrew manuscripts and all the versions put the verb in the singular, giving much less will your god deliver you.

Two further details belong to Ellicott alone. He observes that Assyrian kings are given to invoking their predecessors as this one does, and that the chronicler drops the list of conquered states which Kings preserves, probably because some had grown obscure with time. For the boast about carrying off the gods he cites Assurbanipal, who records taking the gods and goddesses of Elam to Assyria with the rest of the spoil and names nineteen of them. Gill, characteristically brief, reduces the opening taunt to its question: on what power, in heaven or on earth, do you rely.
16:
Ellicott keeps drawing attention to the compression. The note that more was spoken shows the writer does not pretend to a full report, and the letters mentioned next are frankly out of place: they were sent after the first embassy failed, so on a strict sequence the verse would stand after the shouting rather than before it. He treats it as a parenthesis dropped into the account of the envoys, allowing that abbreviation has its necessities. Gill simply refers the reader to the fuller narratives.

On the shouting from below the wall, Ellicott observes that the Greek and Latin make it one speaker, the Rabshakeh, where the Hebrew has several, a point Gill covers by naming him the chief speaker and recalling that the envoys had been asked to use Syriac. The stated purpose, to frighten and unnerve the defenders so the city might be taken, Ellicott identifies as the chronicler's own summary of the long speech reported elsewhere, and he notes that the verb for frightening is rare. He makes the same kind of point about the following verse: rather than repeat the terms offered to the people, this writer fixes on the blasphemy, because that is what brought the Assyrian down. Gill glosses the phrase about the God of Jerusalem as meaning the only living and true God, worshipped in the temple there.

Both Gill and Ellicott note that the parallel accounts do not actually say the prophet prayed. Gill infers that he must have, since the king had asked it and since an answer came through him; Ellicott points to the deputation of nobles sent to request his prayers for the remnant, and refers the phrase upon this to the blasphemies themselves, which the prayer urged as its ground.

What the angel was is answered four ways. Gill reports the Targum, which makes it the Word of the Lord sending Gabriel, then Josephus, who took the messenger for the pestilence, then those who identify it with the Samiel, the poison wind of the east that travellers describe as killing multitudes at a stroke; he declines to choose, holding only that it came from God and did exactly what had been foretold. Wesley gives the Jewish comment in fuller form, Gabriel again, the execution done by lightning, and the night the passover night, the very night the firstborn of Egypt died. Delitzsch stays with the text and observes that no number is given because the number did not matter, the point being that the host was annihilated. Ellicott supplies the number from Kings, a hundred and eighty-five thousand, renders the verb as caused to disappear, and reports Hitzig's suggestion that three psalms were written by Isaiah to commemorate the event, an idea he thinks supported by the kinship between their language and the prophet's.

Over the closing comment the two close readers contradict each other outright. The clause about guiding them round about is unusual, and Ellicott judges a proposed emendation to gave them rest round about to be correct, citing the Greek and Latin and the chronicler's fondness for that phrase elsewhere. Delitzsch defends the received text, taking the verb to mean leading with care and so protecting, and rejects the same conjecture on the ground that the supposed scribal slip is improbable. He also resists adding the word enemies where Ellicott thinks it has dropped out. On the aftermath they agree: the many who brought gifts were chiefly neighbouring peoples, themselves relieved of a dreaded enemy and moved to honour the God who had destroyed him. Clarke puts their motive drily, that they saw whose friend the king was and had no wish to make an enemy of such a man; Ellicott counts the Babylonian envoys among them. Henry closes on the same note he struck at the beginning, that by the favour of God enemies are lost and friends gained.
24:
All the witnesses notice how much is packed into one verse. Ellicott says flatly that it epitomises two long chapters elsewhere, Delitzsch calls what is left mere hints, and Gill and Clarke both simply send the reader to the fuller narratives. Delitzsch adds a small grammatical point, that the speaking and the giving have the same subject, God, so that the prayer is answered by a word through the prophet and by a sign together; Ellicott names the prophet as the mouth used and observes that the Hebrew puts the sign first for emphasis. On what the sign was, Ellicott specifies the shadow going back on the dial of Ahaz, Henry the sun retreating ten degrees, and Henry alone stresses that the illness looked certain to be fatal.

What the pride consisted in is answered with unusual agreement. Delitzsch points to the promise made in the sickness, to walk humbly all his days, and to its breach after recovery, locating the breach in the display of the treasures to the Babylonian embassy and in an idle confidence both in that alliance and in his own resources. Clarke says the same more shortly, a vain confidence and a vain showing of his wealth. Wesley enumerates three things that turned his head, the prodigious victory, the miraculous recovery, and the honour of an embassy from so great a king, and suspects the root of it was a notion that these had been given him for his piety. Henry sharpens that into an epigram: having destroyed the other idolatries, the man began to idolize himself, and he made the very favours he had received the food and fuel of his pride.

The wrath that followed is read by both close readers as a specific thing rather than a mood. Delitzsch and Ellicott alike identify it with the prophecy that the royal treasures would go to Babylon and that some of his sons would serve as eunuchs in the palace there, Delitzsch wondering whether a threat in Micah belongs with it. Both also explain why Judah and Jerusalem are included, since the people shared the king's confidence in an arm of flesh. Henry presses the principle instead, that pride is a sin God hates particularly in his own people, that it drew wrath on David when he numbered the people, and that a heart-sin is still to be repented of though nothing worse comes of it; he notes too that subjects may have to mourn for the sins of their rulers, and that the citizens humbled themselves either because they knew they had shared the fault or because they feared they would share the punishment.

What the humbling actually was gets three different answers, none of them certain. Gill admits the text does not say and guesses at sackcloth, fasting, prayer and confession. Clarke describes an inward motion instead, a man waking from sleep, grieved at his sin and deprecating the anger he had drawn. Ellicott identifies it with something recorded rather than imagined, the reply to the prophet that the word spoken was good, with its acknowledgement that there would at least be peace in his own days.

On the outcome there is no dispute. Delitzsch states it plainly: the judgment was not cancelled but postponed, and fell on the royal house and the whole kingdom only later, in the Chaldean invasion. Henry makes the same point pastorally, that repentance may put by, or at any rate put off, the tokens of anger, and that while this king lived the country kept peace and truth.
27:
Both close readers set the wealth in a series. Delitzsch and Ellicott alike compare the same three predecessors, David, Solomon and Jehoshaphat, who are described in almost these terms, so that the notice is formulaic praise rather than a fresh observation. Gill supplies the sources of the money, the spoil of the Assyrian camp and the presents that came afterwards from the neighbours. On the contents of the treasuries, Delitzsch takes the shields as standing for weapons generally and connects the collection with the armoury that Kings and Isaiah mention; Ellicott makes the same substitution, recalling the golden shields of Solomon and the brazen ones of Rehoboam, and renders the last item literally as vessels of desire, which Clarke also gives in that form, meaning costly implements and utensils of every kind.

The agricultural provision draws out two philological notes and one textual suspicion. Delitzsch derives the word for storehouses from a root meaning to heap up and treats it as a transposition, and he does the same with the word for stalls, which occurs here in a form found nowhere else and must be a metathesis of the usual one. Ellicott lists the cognate forms and then observes that the last two words of the verse look transposed by a copyist, since the Hebrew as it stands says flocks for folds where the Greek and Latin both read folds for the flocks.

The cities are the real crux. Delitzsch denies the word can mean cities in this context and offers two possibilities, watch-towers, from a root meaning to keep watch, or simply dwellings for the herdsmen, noting that the term covers any enclosed place from a tower to a walled town. Ellicott settles on the first, translating outright that he made himself watch-towers, forts to protect the flocks and herds. Gill keeps the ordinary sense and supplies the reasoning, that these were the places where the storehouses and stalls stood, with lodgings for the men who managed them, and he mentions a reading in some copies of the Vulgate that specifies six of them. Wesley takes the verb as repairing and fortifying existing towns for the honour and safety of the kingdom.

On the waterworks the accounts converge and then add detail. Delitzsch and Ellicott both describe the upper outlet being closed in and the water carried underground to the west of the city of David, Ellicott pointing out that Kings refers to the same undertaking in its own closing summary and that this writer supplies further particulars. Both also discuss the verb for conducting, which appears in an unusual contracted form in the margin. Clarke speaks plainly of canals cut to bring the water from the west side of the city. Wesley distinguishes the two streams, the upper gathered into what Isaiah calls the upper pool and the lower into another, and says it was the upper that was diverted and piped into the city, calling it a work of great art and labour. Gill is the only one who has been there, or nearly so: he cites the identification of Gihon with Siloam and quotes Maundrell's measurement of the pool outside the Bethlehem gate, a hundred and six paces by sixty-seven, lined with wall and plaster and well stored with water when he saw it.

Henry gathers the whole paragraph under one head. These works belong to the honour God gave the man while he lived, and the diversion of the stream in particular was undertaken when the Assyrian came; the new gathering of the water served the city better than the old pool had. That he prospered in all his works, Henry adds, is said because the works were good ones.
31:
The connective matters more than the English suggests. Delitzsch insists the Hebrew particle never carries an adversative sense, adopts Bertheau's rendering and accordingly, and explains its work: it reconciles an episode that was no part of the king's good fortune with the statement that he prospered in everything. Ellicott arrives at the same place by paraphrase, and thus, meaning while things stood so prosperously with him. Both read the embassy not as an exception to the prosperity but as something that grew out of it.

Why the envoys came is answered four ways. Gill rejects two explanations before giving his own, dismissing the Targum's notion that they came to see the tables of stone in the ark, the broken ones included, and Grotius's view that they asked about the destruction of the Assyrians; he holds it was the sun's retreat they wanted explained, the Chaldeans being much given to astrology. Wesley allows either the destruction or the sign. Henry takes both and supplies a motive for each: the Assyrians were their enemies and their fall worth rejoicing over, while the sun was their god and they would honour a man their god had honoured. Ellicott observes that this errand appears in no parallel account but fits what the monuments show of Babylon, the home of divination, where the temple astronomers would have found such a sign of particular interest; he names the sender, Merodach-baladan, and calls the plural princes of Babylon another of this book's vague rhetorical plurals.

On the leaving alone, Ellicott is careful about what the words can mean. The verb for trying is the ordinary one for tempting, and the clause about knowing must mean bringing to light what was latent, since the Searcher of hearts knew the outcome already; we can only picture such dealings by analogy, as with a chemist putting an imperfectly known substance through combinations to find out its nature. He notes the remark is peculiar to this writer. Delitzsch says the permission was given not to ruin but to humble him. Wesley and Henry both turn it into warning, Henry with the sharpest formulation of the chapter, that God left him to be proud of his wealth in order to keep him from being proud of his holiness. Clarke draws the same lesson from the Targum's gentler version, where the Word of the Lord merely permits the showing and the king does not suffer for it, adding that to know one's own weakness is the beginning of watchfulness.

Over the sources the two close readers part company. Delitzsch takes the vision of Isaiah for the book of that prophet's prophecies, a work distinct from the chronicle of the kings. Ellicott deletes the conjunction and makes the vision a section within the book of the kings of Judah and Israel, noting that Kings itself cites only its own chronicle. Gill glosses the king's goodness as his acts of piety and liberality, which Delitzsch and Ellicott render pious or good deeds.

The burial notice divides them again. Delitzsch reads it as on the height of the graves of the sons of David and guesses the hereditary vault was full, so higher ground had to be used for this king and his successors. Ellicott prefers the ascent, the way up to the royal tombs, and supports the crowding by noting that the next three kings were not buried there either; he adds that these closing statements appear in no canonical parallel and so argue for a source besides Kings. Clarke reads the same words simply as respect paid to the best king since David. On the honour itself Delitzsch and Ellicott agree in conjecturing a great burning of spices, and Wesley ends where Henry does, that a debt is owed to those who have been eminently useful, to honour them at their death when they are beyond the reach of flattery.
